I used to catch horny toads when I was a kid, back when my family would go to visit my stepfather's relatives in Lamesa, Texas.  They were abundant on ranch roads and around barns just outside of town, and during the earlier part of the 1980's you could still catch them running around in backyards and alleys right in the middle of the town.  Harvester ants were also abundant.  The last time I remember collecting around the house was 1987, when this photo was taken.  I remember the house was within a few blocks of the football stadium.  Have not been out there since 1990.  I remember my stepdad's grandfather, who was about 103 years old when he died around 1984, asked me not to keep them because they would die (I was a little kid and of course I wanted to take them back to Dallas with me).  He convinced me not to after telling me that he didn't see nearly as many of them as he used to, and that the ones in his yard (a dry sandy / gravelly yard with a few watered pair trees, some cacti and shrubs) were his pets.  It seems like even then that something might have been happening to them because I noticed fewer of them as I got a little older.  This one photographed next to a penny looks like a hatchling.  I have to admit that I don't know exactly what day the photo was taken, but his family reunions (when we went out to visit) were always in the last week of August.  I would put a + / - five days on this observation.

description: The horned lizard ran off shortly after I snapped the picture. It was near an overgrown fence line with Tamulipan mixed brush growing through it. The soils included more clay than surrounding areas. Dominant species included mesquite, huisache, Kleberg bluestem, prickly pear and lamb's quarter..
The horned lizard was near a community of 15-20 year old mesquites with prickly pear and Kleberg bluestem scattered throughout.

The horned lizard was in the middle of a 100+ meter opening in the brush mottes. Mottes were characterized by mature mesquite trees surrounded by smaller granjenos, whitebrush, and brasil. Common grasses in between included Kleberg bluestem, tanglehead, seacoast bluestem and switchgrass.

The horned lizard was on the side of a caliche road. One of the ranch hands caught the lizard and brought it over to me and the ranch owner. He said that the horned lizard was one of the first he had seen in 2-3 years. This was 4-5 months after all cattle were pulled from the property. Prior to removal of cattle, the property had been moderately overgrazed since 1954. Overgrazing was severe  from 2008-2012 while the land was managed using "alternative methods". Common species surrounding sighting include Hall's panicum, bermuda grass, guajillo, cinema, blackbrush, prickly pear, Spanish dagger, and flowering dogweed.

description: Texas Horned Lizard at Pines Spring Visitor Center; Guadalupe Mountains National Park

This one lives by our shed in the backyard. Behind the shed is a wood pile and 2 trees are on either side of it. It will run into the wood pile if startled. There is also an ant pile of big red ants that have been in our backyard in this area for more than 15 years so we consistently see horned lizards in this area yearly. We have at least 2 big red ant (harvester?) piles in our backyard.

This one lives very close to our back door. It is usually seen under our old bikes (4 bikes leaned against each other) which is next to our bushes that provide a leafy substrate that is easy for it to hide quickly under when startled.

This is just one of multiple immature that reside on the side of our house. The side of our house is lined by bushes and rosebushes which they take shelter under. On this day we saw this one and one more in the same place.
This is the second immature that was with the other one I posted. They were in the same area, in the bushes on the west side of our house. It was scurrying away, so the picture is blurry.

It lives under the mesquite in the front yard, near a large big red ant pile that has been there for many years (+15). We have always observed that at least one horned lizard always inhabits this area.
This photo was taken by my mother. She saw it in the front yard on the west facing side of our house where there are many bushes they have been seen to inhabit.

The Texas horned lizard belongs to the Phrynosomatidae family. An interesting fact about the lizard is when threatened by a predator it puffs up and appears very fat, which causes his body skills to protrude making it difficult to swallow for predators. This picture was taken in Van Horn Texas on a field biology trip.
